title: What makes a city grow?
essentialQuestion: Why do some small settlements become major cities?
learningGoal: Explain how jobs, transport, services and population affect each other as a city grows.

warmUp.question: Why might people move from a village to a city?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What changed first in Bayview, and what happened after that?

events.text: About 2,000 people live in Bayview. Most families fish. There is one harbour and one market.
A new road to the capital city opens. A cold-storage building opens to keep fish fresh. There are 800 new jobs. About 5,000 people now live in Bayview.
About 12,000 people live in Bayview. There are new houses, a new school and bus routes. People wait a long time at the only clinic.

sections.heading: Jobs and transport bring people
sections.text: Most cities start small. A town often grows when something brings new jobs, such as a harbour, a railway or factories. Better transport also helps, because it lets people and goods move in and out more easily. Look at Bayview. In Year 8, a new road and a cold-storage building opened, so fish could stay fresh all the way to the capital city. That created 800 new jobs, and people moved to Bayview to do them. This kind of change is called urbanisation: more and more people come to live in towns and cities.
sections.simpler: Most cities start small. A town can grow when new jobs come. A harbour, a railway or factories can bring jobs. Good transport helps people and goods move. Look at Bayview. In Year 8, a new road opened. A big cold room opened too. It kept fish fresh. This made 800 new jobs. People moved to Bayview for the jobs. This is called urbanisation. More people live in towns and cities.

sections.heading: Real cities grew in similar ways
sections.text: Many real cities grew in a similar way. Nairobi, the capital of Kenya, began in 1899 as a stop on a new railway. Workers and traders came, and the stop slowly grew into a city. Shenzhen, in southern China, was a small city of about 30,000 people in 1980. Then the government made it a special area for business. Factories opened, and millions of people moved there for work. Today it is one of the biggest cities in China. In both places, new jobs and transport made the population grow quickly.
sections.simpler: Real cities grew like this too. Nairobi is a big city in Kenya. It started in 1899 as a stop on a railway. Workers and traders came. The stop grew into a city. Shenzhen is a city in China. In 1980, it was small. Then many factories opened there. Millions of people came to work. Now it is one of China's biggest cities. In both places, jobs and transport made the population grow.

sections.heading: Growth brings benefits and pressures
sections.text: Growth can be good for a city, because a bigger city can have more jobs, schools, shops and buses. But more people also need more homes, clean water and health care. A service is help that people need, like a clinic or a school. Infrastructure means the basic systems a place needs, such as roads, water pipes and power lines. Both take time and money to build. In Year 15, Bayview has new houses, a school and bus routes. But people wait a long time at the only clinic, because it did not grow as fast as the population. Good planners watch for pressures like this and plan ahead.
sections.simpler: Growth can be good. A big city has more jobs, schools and buses. But more people need more things. They need homes and clean water. They need a service like a clinic. They need infrastructure, like roads and pipes. These take time to build. In Year 15, people wait a long time at the Bayview clinic. It did not grow as fast as the population. Planners try to see problems early.

glossary.definition: When more and more people come to live in towns and cities.
glossary.example: Bayview growing from 2,000 to 12,000 people is an example of urbanisation.

glossary.definition: Ways to move people and goods, like buses, trains and boats.
glossary.example: The new road gave Bayview better transport to the capital city.

glossary.definition: The number of people who live in a place.
glossary.example: Bayview's population grew from 2,000 in Year 1 to 12,000 in Year 15.

glossary.definition: Help that people need, like health care, schools or buses.
glossary.example: The clinic is a service that Bayview needs to make bigger.

glossary.definition: Basic systems a place needs, like roads, water pipes and power lines.
glossary.example: The new road in Bayview is part of its infrastructure.

checks.question: What first made Bayview grow quickly?

options.feedback: Not quite. The timeline does not say there were fewer boats. Look at what opened in Year 8.
Not quite. A new road opened. It was not taken away. Look at what opened in Year 8.

options.text: A new road and new jobs
options.feedback: Yes. In Year 8, the new road and cold-storage building made 800 new jobs. People moved to Bayview for them.

checks.question: What do the long waits at the Bayview clinic tell you?

options.text: Growth never brings any problems at all
options.feedback: Not quite. The long waits are a problem. Look for the answer about the clinic and the population.

options.text: The clinic did not grow fast enough
options.feedback: Yes. The population grew to 12,000, but the clinic did not grow as fast. So people wait a long time.

options.text: Many people are leaving Bayview now
options.feedback: Not quite. The population grew to 12,000. People did not leave. Look for the answer about the clinic.

write.prompt: Explain how one change in Bayview led to other changes. Include one benefit of the growth and one pressure it caused.
selfCheck: I showed how one change led to another.
I named one benefit of the growth.
I named one pressure and used evidence from the timeline.
write.example: When the new road opened in Year 8, fish could reach the capital city while they were still fresh. Because of this, there were 800 new jobs. This meant that many people moved to Bayview, and the population grew to 12,000 by Year 15. One benefit was new houses, a new school and bus routes. However, one pressure was the long wait at the clinic, because it did not grow as fast as the town.

speak.partnerTask: Tell your partner one benefit of Bayview's growth. Your partner names one pressure and one way to deal with it.
speak.independentTask: Say the chain aloud: 'Because ___ changed, ___ happened, which meant ___.'

watch.title: Urbanization and the future of cities
watch.why: It explains how cities grew over about 10,000 years and what cities will need as they keep growing.
watch.beforeQuestion: What might make people move from the countryside to a growing city?
watch.afterQuestion: What do growing cities need besides more homes?
watch.summary: The video starts with a fact: today, more than half of all people live in towns and cities. About 10,000 years ago, people began to farm. They could grow food, so they stayed in villages. Later, better farming made extra food. Not everyone had to farm, so some people did other jobs. Villages grew into cities. Trade grew too, with carts, ships, roads and ports. Much later, factories and new machines helped cities grow even bigger. Cities added police, fire services, roads and ways to take away waste. In the future, even more people will live in cities. The video says cities must give everyone enough food, toilets and schools. They must also protect the land. Ideas include rooftop gardens, tall buildings, and power from the sun and wind.
keyPoints: Farming and extra food let villages grow into the first cities.
Trade, transport and later factories helped cities grow bigger.
Future cities will need enough food, toilets and schools for many more people.

visual.description: A three-step picture timeline of the fictional town Bayview, with arrows between the steps. Year 1: a small fishing harbour with boats, one market stall and a few houses, labelled '2,000 people'. Year 8: a new road leading inland and a cold-storage building by the harbour, labelled '5,000 people, 800 new jobs'. Year 15: many more houses, a school, a bus and a small clinic with a long line of people outside, labelled '12,000 people'.
visual.alt: Timeline of the fictional town Bayview growing from a small fishing harbour to a busy town with a new road, a school, buses and a crowded clinic.

sources.label: TED-Ed: Urbanization and the future of cities

educatorNotes: Some learners may have moved between towns or cities themselves. Keep the talk on Bayview and the real examples, and don't ask why learners or their families moved.
Nairobi and Shenzhen are real examples. You could swap in a nearby city learners know, such as Jakarta, if you have a reliable source for how it grew.
The video is from 2013. Its figures (for example, 'more than half of all people live in cities') are still broadly true, but UN numbers change as definitions change, so avoid precise percentages.
changes: Expanded the 87-word reading to three sections: jobs and transport, real examples, and benefits and pressures.
Added real examples from Kenya (Nairobi, a railway stop in 1899) and China (Shenzhen, a small city in 1980).
Kept the fictional Bayview timeline and added what changed in each year.
Rewrote simpler English at about grade 3.
Glossary: kept urbanisation (now British spelling), population, infrastructure and service, and added transport. Every word now appears in the text.
Moved the correct answers to third and second positions and evened out option lengths.
Added starters, a three-item self-check and a longer example answer; rewrote the video summary from the video's narration.
